name: Rievaulx Abbey
date: c.1225 to 1250, abbey founded 1132, nave c.1135 to 1145
materials: Local sandstone ashlar, roofs long gone
description: The eastern arm of a Cistercian abbey suppressed in 1538 and left to fall, which is why you can read its structure so clearly. The nave of the 1130s and 40s is the austere early Cistercian building, low and plain. The presbytery standing here is the rebuilding of about 1225 to 1250, three storeys of it, and it abandons Cistercian plainness completely: tall clustered piers, deeply undercut mouldings and lancet windows in tiers. The roofless state is not decay alone but deliberate stripping of the lead at the Dissolution.
how_to_date_it: Read the piers. Clustered shafts with fillets, set close and rising unbroken through the arcade, plus lancets without any bar tracery, put this in the second quarter of the thirteenth century. Cistercian work of the 1130s and 40s next door is squat, round arched and stripped of ornament, so the two phases sit side by side on one site.

name: Whitby Abbey
date: c.1220 to 1250, north transept later 13th century, Anglian monastery founded 657
architect: Benedictine masons, patron the de Percy family
location: Abbey Lane, Whitby, North Yorkshire YO22 4JT
materials: Local sandstone ashlar, roofless since the Dissolution
description: The gaunt shell of a Benedictine church on the headland above the harbour, standing on the site of the double monastery founded in 657 where Caedmon sang and the Synod of Whitby met in 664. Nothing of the Anglian house survives above ground. What you see is the thirteenth century rebuilding: a tall presbytery of three storeys with lancets in tiers, then a north transept in a slightly later and more elaborate manner. The nave fell in 1763, the central tower in 1830, and the west front was shelled by German battlecruisers in 1914.
how_to_date_it: Tiers of tall narrow lancets with no bar tracery, clustered shafts and dogtooth ornament in the mouldings are Early English, roughly 1200 to 1260. Where the tracery becomes geometrical, with circles and foiled shapes in the window head, you have moved into the later thirteenth century work.

name: Radcliffe Camera
architect: James Gibbs for the trustees of Dr John Radcliffe
materials: Headington and Burford limestone ashlar with a lead covered timber dome
description: England's first round library, and the building that gives central Oxford its silhouette. Gibbs set a rusticated octagonal base under a circular upper storey ringed with paired Corinthian columns, then a balustrade, then a lead dome on a drum. It is a Baroque composition built at a moment when fashionable London had already moved on to cool Palladian correctness, which is why it feels theatrical next to Holkham or Chiswick of the same decade. The reading room inside is a single domed rotunda.
how_to_date_it: Paired columns, deep rustication and a dome on a drum are Baroque, but the crisp dry cutting and the absence of Vanbrugh's weight place this a generation later, in the 1730s and 40s. Gibbs was Scottish, Rome trained and Catholic, and stayed Baroque long after Burlington's circle had abandoned it.

name: Kensington Palace
architect: Sir Christopher Wren for William III and Mary II; later work by Colen Campbell and William Benson
materials: Red and brown brick with rubbed brick dressings, Portland stone and a lead roof
description: Not a palace built as one, but a Jacobean merchant's house at Kensington that William III bought in 1689 because Whitehall's river air ruined his asthma. Wren wrapped pavilions round it at speed, in brick rather than stone, because the King wanted a private house and not a state one. The result is domestic in scale and materials and set the tone for English court building for a generation. The south front here carries giant brick pilasters against darker stock brick, a dentilled cornice and an attic centrepiece with urns.
how_to_date_it: Brick doing the work of a stone order, giant pilasters in rubbed red brick against browner stock, and a wooden dentilled cornice rather than a carved entablature, is the William and Mary court manner of about 1690 to 1700. Beware the windows: many of these sashes were reglazed later, so the bars are thinner than they should be for the 1690s.

name: Oxburgh Hall
architect: Built for Sir Edmund Bedingfeld; Victorian remodelling by J C Buckler and others
materials: Red brick with dark blue diaper patterning and limestone dressings, set in a moat
description: A moated brick manor house begun in 1482 under a licence to crenellate, and still owned by the family that built it. The gatehouse is the great survival: seven storeys of brick with polygonal turrets, a four centred arch and diaper patterning in burnt headers, built for display rather than defence at the point when brick was still an expensive imported taste in England. Much of the rest was heavily remodelled in the nineteenth century in a Tudor manner, so the house is a lesson in telling real late medieval brick from Victorian sympathy.
how_to_date_it: Late medieval brick shows dark blue diaper patterns made from over burnt headers, four centred arches, moulded brick mullions and crow stepped or shaped gables, with no classical detail anywhere. Victorian Tudor next to it is too even: machine pressed brick of uniform colour, sharp arrises and larger panes of glass.

name: SIS Building (Vauxhall Cross)
architect: Terry Farrell and Partners for the Secret Intelligence Service
materials: Precast concrete cladding in a sand colour, with green tinted triple glazing and bronze anodised metalwork
description: Farrell's headquarters for MI6 on the south bank at Vauxhall, and the most conspicuous secret building in Britain. The massing is a stepped ziggurat, symmetrical about a central tower, with the setbacks reading as a temple platform borrowed from Mesopotamia by way of nineteen thirties cinema architecture. The green glass and sand coloured precast are chosen for effect rather than structure, and the whole thing is armoured, with blast resistant glazing and a moat like sunken perimeter. It has been blown up on screen more often than any other London building.
how_to_date_it: Stepped ziggurat massing, symmetry, coloured glass and precast panels imitating stone are Postmodernism, roughly 1985 to 1995. It is easily told from High Tech of the same years, which exposes structure and services, and from Brutalism twenty years earlier, which leaves raw concrete poured in place.

name: Pierhead Building
architect: William Frame for the Bute Dock Company
location: Pierhead Street, Cardiff Bay, Cardiff CF10 4PZ
materials: Bright red Ruabon terracotta and brick with slate roofs
description: Built as the headquarters of the Bute Dock Company at the height of Cardiff's coal boom, when the city was shipping more coal than anywhere on earth. William Frame trained under William Burges and the debt shows: a French Gothic Renaissance pile in vivid red terracotta, with a hexagonal clock tower, steep slated roofs, corner turrets and a parade of moulded panels and gargoyles. The clock was known as Baby Big Ben. It survived the docks' collapse and now stands almost alone as the Victorian survivor among the new buildings of Cardiff Bay.
how_to_date_it: Machine moulded terracotta in a uniform bright red, with the same ornament repeated bay after bay, is post 1870 and usually 1880 to 1905. French Gothic detail on a commercial office, rather than a church or a town hall, points to the confident dock and railway companies of the 1890s.

name: Eilean Donan Castle
date: 1912 to 1932, on a castle destroyed in 1719
architect: Reconstructed for Lieutenant Colonel John MacRae-Gilstrap; architect George Mackie Watson
location: Dornie, Kyle of Lochalsh, Highland IV40 8DX
materials: Coursed local rubble with harling, slate roofs, concrete floors behind
description: The most photographed castle in Scotland and almost entirely a twentieth century building. A stronghold stood on the islet from the thirteenth century, but it was blown up by Royal Navy frigates in 1719 during the Jacobite rising and lay as a low heap of rubble for nearly two hundred years. MacRae-Gilstrap bought the island in 1911 and rebuilt from 1912 to 1932, working partly from a set of plans said to have come to a stonemason in a dream. The arched bridge is part of the reconstruction. Behind the medieval manner are concrete floors and twentieth century services.
how_to_date_it: The tells are all in the regularity. Rubble coursed too evenly, window openings of matching size marching across the wall, plate glass in every one of them and crisp square arrises on the dressings. Genuine medieval work is irregular, has very few openings and those are small, deep and unequal. If a castle looks complete and comfortable, suspect a rebuild.

name: Terrace with the Headington Shark
architect: Speculative builder unknown; shark by John Buckley for Bill Heine
location: 2 New High Street, Headington, Oxford OX3 7AQ
materials: Red brick with slate roof, timber sash windows and small gabled porches
description: An entirely ordinary Victorian terrace in an Oxford suburb, with a seven metre fibreglass shark head first through the roof. Bill Heine had it installed on 9 August 1986, the forty first anniversary of Nagasaki, without permission. Oxford City Council fought to remove it for six years, and the case went to the Secretary of State, whose inspector ruled that the shark could stay. In 2022 the house was given Grade II listing status by the council as a building of local interest, shark included, which is the only reason most people have ever looked closely at a row like this.
how_to_date_it: Ignore the shark and read the terrace. Two storeys of red brick with segmental arches over the openings, plain stone or brick cills, a low pitched slate roof and paired sashes are the speculative builder's standard from the 1860s onward. Once the glazing bars have gone from the sashes, leaving one or two panes, you are after about 1855.

name: Trellick Tower
architect: Ernő Goldfinger for the Greater London Council
location: Golborne Road, Kensal Town, London W10 5PL
materials: Board marked in situ and precast reinforced concrete, thirty one storeys
description: Goldfinger's last and largest building, and the twin of his earlier Balfron Tower in Poplar. The plan separates living from servicing completely: flats in the slab, and lifts, stairs, rubbish chutes and the boiler house in a detached tower linked by bridges every third floor, which lets the flats run through the building and get light from both sides. It was vandalised and feared through the 1980s, listed in 1998, and is now sought after. The top of the service tower holds the boiler house, which is why the silhouette is so odd.
how_to_date_it: Board marked concrete left raw, a service tower held away from the slab and joined by bridges, and deep recessed balconies are British Brutalism of roughly 1965 to 1975. Fifties towers are lighter and thinner with tiled or rendered panels; eighties towers hide their concrete behind cladding or brick.

name: Norfolk and Suffolk Terraces, University of East Anglia
architect: Sir Denys Lasdun for the University of East Anglia
materials: Precast and in situ reinforced concrete with continuous glazing to the stepped terraces
description: Student residences stepped down the valley of the Yare in a zigzag section, universally known as the Ziggurats. Each study bedroom gets its own terrace from the step of the one below, and the breakfast rooms sit in the projecting glazed prows. Lasdun called his approach architecture as strata and landscape, and it is the same idea he took to the National Theatre a few years later, worked out here first. The service towers rising above the terraces carry the stairs and plant.
how_to_date_it: A stepped section where every floor is set back to make a terrace, in raw concrete with continuous glazing along each step, is British Brutalism of about 1960 to 1972. Lasdun's work is recognisably horizontal, built up in layers rather than composed as towers, which sets it apart from the point blocks of the same years.

name: Quay House, the Smallest House in Great Britain
location: The Quay, Conwy, Conwy County Borough LL32 8BB
materials: Rubble stone with lime render, slate roof, painted red
description: A one up one down infill house wedged against the town wall on Conwy quay, 3.05 metres by 1.8 metres, with a staircase too narrow for its last tenant, a fisherman of six foot three who could not stand upright in it. Condemned as unfit in 1900 and saved as a curiosity by the owner, who toured Britain to prove nothing smaller existed. It is a scrap of ordinary sixteenth century town building that survived only by being too odd to demolish, which is the opposite of how the rest of this list survived.
how_to_date_it: Small town vernacular barely changes for two hundred years, so read it as a wide bracket rather than a decade. Rubble walls, a steep slate pitch, tiny unequal openings and a chimney enormous in proportion to the plan are pre Georgian, roughly 1500 to 1750. Regular sashes and symmetry on the neighbours are the later refronting.

name: Wales Millennium Centre
architect: Jonathan Adams of Percy Thomas Architects; inscription by Gwyneth Lewis
location: Bute Place, Cardiff Bay, Cardiff CF10 5AL
materials: Bronzed stainless steel shell over a steel frame, with banded Welsh slate from Penrhyn, Ffestiniog and Corris, and glass
description: A national arts centre built for Wales after an earlier opera house scheme was abandoned, and designed to look like it grew out of the ground it stands on. The slate is laid in bands of different Welsh quarries so the walls read as strata, and the bronzed shell above is meant to suggest the hull of a ship on a dock that once shipped coal. Gwyneth Lewis's two lines, one Welsh and one English, are cut clean through the shell so they light the foyer by day and glow at night. The lettering is the building's structure, not applied to it.
how_to_date_it: Millennium buildings of about 1998 to 2010 look like this: a curved metal shell over a fully glazed public frontage, regionally sourced material used symbolically rather than structurally, and a big legible gesture aimed at civic identity. It is a generation past High Tech, which exposes its services, and past Postmodernism, which quotes classical form.

name: Raglan Castle
architect: Begun for Sir William ap Thomas, continued by his son William Herbert, Earl of Pembroke
materials: Old Red Sandstone rubble and ashlar with Bath stone dressings
description: The last true castle built in England or Wales, and one built for magnificence rather than war. Ap Thomas began the hexagonal Great Tower, the Yellow Tower of Gwent, in the 1430s, and his son turned the rest into a courtyard palace with a gatehouse of real swagger. The Somersets added long galleries and formal gardens in the Elizabethan decades. It held out for Parliament's siege in 1646 longer than almost anywhere, and was then deliberately slighted, which is why the Great Tower stands with one side torn away.
how_to_date_it: Look at the windows. Large mullioned and transomed openings in a castle mean the fifteenth century or later, when defence has become display. Machicolations and gunports here are as much ornament as armament, and the tall stacks and traceried hall windows are those of a house wearing a castle's clothes.

name: Broadway Tower
architect: James Wyatt for the 6th Earl of Coventry
materials: Cotswold limestone rubble with ashlar dressings
description: A folly on the second highest point of the Cotswolds, built so the Countess of Coventry could see whether a beacon lit there was visible from her house twenty two miles away. Three round turrets, battlements and gargoyles, none of it defensive.
how_to_date_it: Castle language used ornamentally rather than structurally is the tell. Battlements too thin to stand behind, turrets carrying nothing, and neatly squared ashlar dressings mean Georgian Gothick of about 1780 to 1810, not a real medieval tower.

name: House in the Clouds
architect: F Forbes Glennie for Glencairn Stuart Ogilvie
materials: Weatherboarded timber casing on a steel water tank over a rendered base
description: A water tower for a purpose-built holiday village, disguised as a cottage hoisted seventy feet into the air. The weatherboarded box at the top is the casing round the tank; the rooms are in the tower beneath it.
how_to_date_it: The proportions give it away: no cottage is that narrow and that tall. Weatherboarding, casements and a hipped tiled roof are 1920s cottage vocabulary wrapped round a structure whose real job is engineering.

name: Beach Lighthouse, Fleetwood
architect: Decimus Burton for Sir Peter Hesketh-Fleetwood
description: The lower of two lighthouses set inland along a street, so a ship lining them up is running the safe channel into the Wyre. Part of Burton's planned new town, which is why a navigation light looks like civic architecture.
how_to_date_it: Greek Revival detail on a working structure dates it. A plain ashlar tower on a stepped square base, a correct cornice, and no ornament beyond mouldings: classical proportion applied to infrastructure is 1820 to 1845.

name: Young V&A, Bethnal Green
architect: James William Wild, re-using the iron frame of the 1856 Brompton Boilers
location: Cambridge Heath Road, Bethnal Green, London E2 9PA
materials: Red brick casing over a prefabricated wrought iron and glass frame
description: The iron structure was built at South Kensington in 1856, dismantled, re-erected here and wrapped in a brick shell. The inside is fifteen years older than the outside, and the two are of quite different tempers.
how_to_date_it: Read the inside and outside as separate buildings. Exposed iron columns and roof are prefabricated 1850s exhibition engineering; the plain round-arched brick box round them, with its terracotta frieze, is 1870s.
